card.hook: Picture a row of pastel hotels, and then the neon flickering on just as the sky turns peachy. That's Ocean Drive, and it looks exactly like the postcard in your head.
card.stand_here: Walk to the Colony Hotel at 736 Ocean Drive and stand on the park-side pavement in front of it. Face the hotel so you can fit the lit neon sign, the pastel facade and a strip of dusk sky into one shot.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the sign, the building and some sky in the frame. If the pavement is too narrow to step back, switch to 0.5x and keep the sign away from the edges of the picture.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the sign on an upper third line, and keep your phone upright and level so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Dusk is the sweet spot, when the neon is lit and there's still colour left in the sky. Advice online disagrees: some people like early morning for emptier streets, others prefer night for the neon.
card.selfie_here: Stand on Ocean Drive in front of the Beacon Hotel with its neon-lit facade behind you. Photo guides rank it as the most photographed stretch of the strip, and the neon frames a night selfie well. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone a bit low so the hotel fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Stand in Lummus Park, the park strip between Ocean Drive and the beach, and ask a passer-by to shoot from the beach side so the Art Deco hotel facades show behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Parts of Ocean Drive may be closed to cars at times, so check current street closures before you go. Watch for traffic and keep out of the pedestrian flow while you line up the shot.
card.challenge: Take one photo where the neon sign is the star, then one where you are, and see which one ends up as your lock screen.
card.good_to_know: Ocean Drive is the street most people picture when they think of Miami's Art Deco seafront. It's a row of pastel hotel facades with neon signs that come on as the light fades. The Colony Hotel's lit sign and pastel facade are often named as the most photogenic on the street.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk to the Colony Hotel at 736 Ocean Drive and stand on the park-side pavement in front of it. Face the hotel so you can fit the lit neon sign, the pastel facade and a strip of dusk sky into one shot.

card.hook: A 19,500-seat arena sounds huge, but from the waterfront it can look like just another building in the skyline. Don't worry, that's the charm of this shot.
card.stand_here: Stand on the seawall path in Bayfront Park, facing the bay, with the downtown towers behind you. The arena is a short walk to the north along the waterfront, so turn that way to frame it among the skyline.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the bay and skyline in, then step up to 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the arena closer. You only need zoom 0.5x if you want lots of sky and water.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the arena, then slide it a little darker if the sky is washing out.
card.best_time: Early morning gives soft light and late afternoon gives warm tones. After dark the skyline is lit up, so switch on night mode and rest your elbows on a railing or wall to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Try the Kaseya Center's outdoor veranda, which looks out over Biscayne Bay and downtown Miami. Use the front camera, and I can't promise the arena will be in the background there, so check your frame before you grin.
card.rules_and_safety: The arena's rules ban selfie sticks, drones, outside food and drinks and professional recording equipment, and it's unclear if that covers the outdoor areas, so leave the stick behind if you're heading to an event. Bayfront Park is free and photography is allowed, but the arena is a ticketed venue, so check the official site before you go. On match and concert days it gets busy, so keep your phone close and look around before you step back to frame a shot.
card.challenge: Get the arena into your shot off-centre, with the water along the bottom third and the skyline above it.
card.good_to_know: The arena opened on 31 December 1999 as American Airlines Arena and has been called Kaseya Center since April 2023. Arquitectonica was one of the design firms behind it. Inside, the scoreboard by artist Christopher Janney is inspired by sea anemones and can change colour with the mood of the event.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the seawall path in Bayfront Park, facing the bay, with the downtown towers behind you. The arena is a short walk to the north along the waterfront, so turn that way to frame it among the skyline.

card.hook: Here's the funny thing about Vizcaya: you're only a few steps from a whole villa, and it still won't fit on your screen. Pale stone, carved detail and clipped greenery are all packed into one frame, so you'll be busy.
card.stand_here: Go to the phone icon on the map at Vizcaya Museum and Gardens. Stand about 20 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east towards the villa.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole facade in, since you're so close. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for doorways, statues and carved stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, tap the brightest part of the facade, then slide it a little darker so the pale stone doesn't turn white.
card.best_time: Softer morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters pale stone better than harsh midday sun. Going early may also mean fewer people in your shots.
card.selfie_here: Head up to the shaded deck at the top of the grand limestone staircases on the Garden Mound, where the gardens spread out below and the bay peeks between the trees. Use the front camera, hold it a little low and keep the view over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by, stand by the central fountain in the Fountain Garden with the Main House behind you, and ask them to shoot from the garden side, angling to keep the house in frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography sessions are allowed in the gardens only, not inside the Main House. Never block paths, gates or walkways, and keep an eye out for passing boats if you're shooting near the barge and the water's edge.
card.challenge: Find a path or flight of steps that leads the eye to the house, then get one shot of the whole facade and one close-up of a doorway or statue.
card.good_to_know: Vizcaya was built as a winter villa for James Deering, and most of it went up between 1914 and 1922. The gardens are laid out as a series of 'rooms', including a Secret Garden, a Theatre Garden, a Maze Garden and a Fountain Garden. It became a National Historic Landmark in 1994.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go to the phone icon on the map at Vizcaya Museum and Gardens. Stand about 20 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east towards the villa.

card.hook: Picture rows of gleaming yachts bobbing in the foreground and a whole city skyline sitting right behind them. That's the marina side of Bayside Marketplace, and it's the picture everyone's after.
card.stand_here: Stand along the docks on the Biscayne Bay side of Bayside Marketplace, at the Miamarina. Face out across the water toward the downtown skyline.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x, which fits the yachts and the skyline in one frame. Try 0.5x for more docks and boats up front, or 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pull the skyline closer or pick out a single boat.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the skyline, then drag the brightness slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Go around sunset, when the skyline is reflected across the bay. Weekend evenings get busy, so arrive a little before sunset and grab a gap along the waterfront.
card.selfie_here: Try the Bayside marina waterfront promenade, along the marina edge, best at sunset. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x, and keep the skyline over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: For a photo of you both, head to Pier 5 on the pier by the marina, where the observation wheel and boats are in view, and ask a passer-by to take it.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is listed as allowed at Bayside Marketplace. The shops and restaurants have their own rules, so check the official site before you go. A guide says the marina, restaurants and park area usually have enough foot traffic that most visitors feel comfortable, even at night.
card.challenge: Catch a boat pulling away from the dock in your frame. Try a Live Photo, then pick your favourite moment afterwards.
card.good_to_know: Bayside Marketplace opened on 8 April 1987. It has two buildings, the North Pavilion and the South Pavilion, on a site of about 16 acres. The architect, Benjamin C. Thompson, gave it the look of old market sheds.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand along the docks on the Biscayne Bay side of Bayside Marketplace, at the Miamarina. Face out across the water toward the downtown skyline.

card.hook: Stand at the edge of Biscayne Bay and you get two photos for the price of one: open water in front of you, and a wall of Miami towers right behind you.
card.stand_here: Walk onto Baywalk, the bayfront path, toward the Bayside Marketplace end of the park. Face the water for the wide bay shot, then turn around for the skyline.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x for the big sweep of bay and sky, then switch to 1x for a more natural look at the towers. Try zoom 2x to 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out the fountain jets or the Torch of Friendship from a distance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and set the horizon on a line, with a bit of water along the bottom of the frame, so everything sits straight and the picture feels deep.
card.best_time: Evening is the one to aim for if you want the fountain, because guides point to its evening light show. The park is big, so leave a little time to walk between spots.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the Torch of Friendship monument inside the park, use the front camera, and keep the Torch over your shoulder. The fountain is the other crowd favourite, especially in the evening light show, so try zoom 0.5x on the front camera to squeeze the jets in behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks are on the prohibited list at the FPL Solar Amphitheater inside the park, though individual events may set their own rules. The park is fully outdoors, so bring sun protection, and check the official site before you go because events can limit access.
card.challenge: Get the fountain jets in the foreground and the towers behind them in one frame, and see if you can catch the spray at its highest.
card.good_to_know: Bayfront Park is a 32-acre park that opened in March 1925, and from 1980 artist and landscape architect Isamu Noguchi reworked it. The Torch of Friendship (1960) stands at the north-west corner, and the 100-foot spiralling steel Challenger Memorial is at the south-west corner. The Pepper Fountain on the eastern side reopened in February 2025 and can throw water up to about 150 feet (46 m).
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk onto Baywalk, the bayfront path, toward the Bayside Marketplace end of the park. Face the water for the wide bay shot, then turn around for the skyline.

card.hook: Here's the fun bit about Wynwood: the mural you spotted online might be painted over by the time you arrive. Don't sulk. Whatever's up on the day is the one you get to record.
card.stand_here: Stand on the sidewalk on NW 2nd Avenue, right in front of the gated Wynwood Walls complex. Face west, toward the outer walls and their big murals, with more mural-covered blocks running off to either side.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so a whole wall fits in from the pavement, and you don't have to step into the road. Then switch to 1x for a cleaner shot of one mural. If your phone has 2x or 5x, use it to pick out details from across the street.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the wall, then slide it a little darker so the paint colours stay rich, and switch on gridlines so the wall's edge lines up with a vertical line.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, before about 11 AM. It's quieter and the shadows are softer. Noon to 3 PM is harsh glare, so skip it if you can.
card.selfie_here: Try the entrance at 2520 NW 2nd Avenue: stand in front of it with the murals and green lawn filling the frame behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a bit low and tilt it up so the walls show over your shoulder. If you go inside, one travel blogger calls the Maya Hayuk mural a popular selfie spot.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photos and videos are allowed, but professional photo shoots need prior approval. Keep walkways clear, don't stand on the painted pavement, and stay on the sidewalk rather than the road.
card.challenge: Get two shots: one wide wall with dead-straight edges, and one close-up of a single mural. Then pick your favourite and call it art criticism.
card.good_to_know: Wynwood Walls is a gated complex of large murals in Miami's Wynwood district, listed at 2516 NW 2nd Ave. The main complex is ticketed, with entry through the Welcome Center on NW 26th Street, so check the official site for hours and rules before you go. The streets outside are public and free to photograph from the pavement.

card.hook: Walk up Ocean Drive and you'll spot the queue before the house: people lining up politely for their turn at the famous front steps. Casa Casuarina, the old Versace Mansion, is formal, symmetrical and made for a straight-on photo.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Ocean Drive sidewalk directly in front of the wrought-iron gates and coquina steps, at 1116 Ocean Drive. Face the gates and keep your phone level so the walls stay straight.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole facade in, steps included. If the sidewalk is too narrow, drop to 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for a medallion, doorway or gate detail.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the gate up with the middle of the frame, so both sides of the facade look even.
card.best_time: Morning light is suggested for showing off the carved stonework. If the sidewalk is busy, wait a moment for a gap in the passers-by.
card.selfie_here: The pale coquina front steps are the star. Time Out calls them the town's most photographed spot. Use the front camera at 0.5x from the sidewalk, with the steps and entrance over your shoulder, and keep it to what's visible from the street.
card.ask_someone: Tour groups queue on the Ocean Drive sidewalk in front of the front steps, so ask someone there to stand on the sidewalk facing the gates while you pose in front of the steps.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a private hotel, so shoot from the public sidewalk. The courtyard, pool and interiors are for hotel guests and diners at Gianni's only.
card.challenge: Take your full-facade shot first, then hunt for one wall medallion and make it the star of a close-up.
card.good_to_know: Casa Casuarina was finished in 1930 for Alden Freeman, a philanthropist and Standard Oil heir, who said he modelled it on the Alcázar de Colón. Gianni Versace lived here from 1992 until 1997. Since 2015 it has been a boutique hotel, The Villa Casa Casuarina, with ten suites.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Ocean Drive sidewalk directly in front of the wrought-iron gates and coquina steps, at 1116 Ocean Drive. Face the gates and keep your phone level so the walls stay straight.

card.hook: Picture standing on top of a giant fish tank with the whole Miami skyline lined up in front of you. That's The Vista, and it's a fun place to be a tourist.
card.stand_here: Go up to The Vista, the open-air rooftop terrace at the top of the Aquarium, and find a spot at the edge. Face the Downtown Miami skyline and Biscayne Bay, with the Port of Miami close by.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the skyline, the bay and the tank surface in one shot. Try 0.5x if you want more terrace and sky, then 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out cruise ships or single towers.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the skyline along the upper third, then tap the skyline and drag the brightness down a little so the sky keeps its colour near sunset.
card.best_time: Try to arrive about an hour before sunset, when the views are reported to be clear and cruise ships may be at the port. Check the official site for rooftop access on the day.
card.selfie_here: At the Oculus, stand at the very bottom of the conical tank on the Deep level with your back to the big round window and the sharks overhead. Up on the rooftop terrace, turn your back on Biscayne Bay and the skyline and use the front camera, or 0.5x to fit more in.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand at the south end of Maurice A. Ferré Park, aiming toward the bay, so the museum and the neighbouring skyscrapers fill the frame with you in it.
card.rules_and_safety: The Vista and the Oculus are inside the museum, so you need a ticket. Flash isn't allowed in the aquarium areas, and planetarium shows generally can't be photographed while they run.
card.challenge: Go indoors to the Oculus, look up through the window, and catch a shark or ray gliding right across the middle. Take a quick burst, because they won't wait for you.
card.good_to_know: The museum opened in Museum Park on 8 May 2017, after the old Coconut Grove museum closed in 2015. It has four interconnected buildings. The star is a three-storey, cone-shaped aquarium holding about 500,000 US gallons.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go up to The Vista, the open-air rooftop terrace at the top of the Aquarium, and find a spot at the edge. Face the Downtown Miami skyline and Biscayne Bay, with the Port of Miami close by.

card.hook: Picture a long, low building that looks like it's floating above the palms, with plants hanging down from its roof like green curtains. That's PAMM, and it's very hard to take a boring picture of it.
card.stand_here: Walk south-west to the sloped lawn of Maurice A. Ferré Park, in front of the museum. Turn around and face the building, and you'll get the whole long front with the lawn and palms below it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x if you're close and want the whole long building in one frame. Step back and switch to 1x for a more natural look. Then try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) for the hanging plant columns and the big staircase.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line the long top edge of the building up with one of them, so it looks nice and level.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and gentler shadows under the canopy. Midday sun is brighter and more contrasty.
card.selfie_here: Try the swings on the outdoor terrace, hanging under the canopy and facing Biscayne Bay, with the museum behind you. Use the front camera and hold it a little above eye level. For a leafy backdrop, stand by the hanging planters near the main entrance instead. Nobody gave us an exact pin for either spot, so look around when you get there.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the park lawn below the museum (take the stairs down from the patio) and frame you with the building behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Turn your flash off. Photography is fine in some areas and not in others, so respect any no-photo signs. Rules inside the galleries can change with each exhibition, so ask staff before you shoot indoors. Museum entry and some grounds may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole building first. Then find three close-ups: a plant column, the staircase, and a shadow under the canopy.
card.good_to_know: The building is by the Swiss architects Herzog & de Meuron and opened in December 2013. The design comes from Stiltsville, the wooden houses on stilts off Key Biscayne, which is why the galleries sit above a deep, shaded veranda. The hanging gardens are by the French botanist Patrick Blanc and use around 80 kinds of plants. The grand staircase to the waterfront is nearly 180 feet wide.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk south-west to the sloped lawn of Maurice A. Ferré Park, in front of the museum. Turn around and face the building, and you'll get the whole long front with the lawn and palms below it.

card.hook: Beach, lawns, passing ships and the downtown Miami skyline all squeeze into one park at the very tip of South Beach. It's hard to run out of things to photograph.
card.stand_here: Walk out onto South Pointe Pier, then turn back toward the park. Face the beach side so the shoreline sits in front of you, with the lifeguard tower and the South Beach hotels behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the shoreline, beach and hotels. Switch to 0.5x to fit in the pier rails and lots of sky. If you turn to face the open sea, try zoom 2x to 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out a ship.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the waterline on a lower third line, so the beach, buildings and sky each get their own space.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning. The pier is recommended for sunrise and the views are clearest then, and weekends can get busy. The shot back toward the park may not show the sun, so turn around if you want it in the picture. For the skyline, the park lawns in the evening are a good choice.
card.selfie_here: Head to the seaward end of South Pointe Pier and face out over the water. The ocean makes a great backdrop, with the Miami skyline stretching out behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if your phone has it to fit more in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the sand just north of the jetty and look south, so the jetty and park area sit in the frame with you in front.
card.rules_and_safety: Access to the pier and its closing times can change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Catch a ship gliding past on the horizon, then spin around and get the lifeguard tower in a second shot.
card.good_to_know: South Pointe Park is 17 acres and opened on 25 October 1985. It was redesigned by Hargreaves Associates, with the work finishing around March 2009. The wide limestone-edged walkways date from that rebuild.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk out onto South Pointe Pier, then turn back toward the park. Face the beach side so the shoreline sits in front of you, with the lifeguard tower and the South Beach hotels behind it.

card.hook: Picture a street with no cars, a line of palm trees and a crowd of people strolling along it. Lincoln Road is one of those places where the street itself is the star.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Lincoln Road and Washington Avenue, the Washington Avenue end of the mall, where a historical marker tells you you're in the right place. Face west and let the whole walkway stretch out in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the long view down the mall. Go to 0.5x if you want more palms and shopfronts along the sides. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a detail, like the front of the Colony Theatre or a row of palms.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and put the middle of the walkway on the centre line, so the shopfronts lead the eye down the street.
card.best_time: Early morning is usually calmer, with fewer people in your frame. Late afternoon and evening bring warmer light and lit-up shops, but you'll be facing the sun, so expect some glare. Tap the middle of the street and slide it a little darker if the sky is too bright.
card.selfie_here: Pose in front of the Lincoln Road Mall sign, a classic shot here. Or head to the fountain at the Colony Theatre, at the end of the pedestrian street, and use the black-and-white striped floor as your backdrop. Use the front camera and hold it a bit lower and wider (0.5x, if your phone has it) to fit the scene behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone near the corner of Lincoln Road and Washington Avenue, next to the Soundscape Park sculptures, to take your photo while you stand on the corner with the mall stretching out behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a busy place, so keep to the side of the walkway when you stop for a photo. The Miami sun can be intense, even at sunrise, so drink water and protect yourself. If your photos are for business, commercial shoots may need a permit, so check the official Miami Beach site first.
card.challenge: Take a few frames in a row and wait for people to wander through the middle of the scene, then pick the one where they look like they're walking straight into your photo.
card.good_to_know: Lincoln Road began in 1912 as a strip cleared through the mangroves. In the 1950s architect Morris Lapidus redesigned it in his playful Miami Modern ("MiMo") style. It opened as a pedestrian mall in November 1960, one of the first in the country, and it's now on the National Register of Historic Places.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Lincoln Road and Washington Avenue, the Washington Avenue end of the mall, where a historical marker tells you you're in the right place. Face west and let the whole walkway stretch out in front of you.

card.hook: Picture a car-free lane with pink and peach buildings, balconies, restaurant tables and strings of lights overhead. The buildings do the framing, so you barely have to try.
card.stand_here: Stand on Española Way in the middle of the pedestrian block and face west, down the lane. The walkway leads away from you, the lights run overhead and the pastel buildings sit on both sides.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the classic view down the lane. Switch to zoom 0.5x to fit the whole lit canopy and both rows of buildings, and keep people away from the edges of the frame, where they can look stretched. Zoom 2x or more packs the string lights closer together.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the lane, then slide it a little darker so the string lights stay bright instead of washing out.
card.best_time: Go at sunset or just after, when the string lights come on and the colours turn soft and warm. After dark, switch on night mode and keep your elbows tucked against your body so the shot stays sharp.
card.selfie_here: Try the corner by Havana 1957, which is described as one of the most photographed corners on the street. Use the front camera with the street behind you. Or stand beside the Don Quijote sculpture at the entrance, with the lane behind you, if it's still there.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Washington Avenue at the mouth of the street while you stand in the lane, so the pedestrian lane runs west behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The lane is pedestrian-only, so there's no traffic to dodge, but it gets busy with outdoor diners after dark, so wait for a gap. Check the official site before you go for any events or closures.
card.challenge: Take the same shot twice, once with the lane empty and once with a few walkers in it, and decide which one wins.
card.good_to_know: South Beach is the part of Miami Beach south of Dade Boulevard. It was the first part of the island to be developed, starting in the 1910s, and it's best known for its 1930s Art Deco, Streamline Moderne and Nautical Moderne buildings. Española Way has a gentler, more Mediterranean look, which makes it a nice contrast to the seafront.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Española Way in the middle of the pedestrian block and face west, down the lane. The walkway leads away from you, the lights run overhead and the pastel buildings sit on both sides.

card.hook: Look down Biscayne Boulevard and your eye goes straight to one slim, decorated tower. The road does half the work for you, which is why this is the postcard angle.
card.stand_here: Stand on Biscayne Boulevard, on the pavement in front of the Freedom Tower's east façade, and face the tower so the wide road leads the eye to it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the front of the tower with the road running to it. If the top gets cut off, try zoom 0.5x and keep your phone level so the tower doesn't lean. Then zoom 2x or more for a close-up of the cupola.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the tower on one of the vertical lines, and leave a little sky above the cupola.
card.best_time: Mid-morning or early evening gives the best light. Come back after dark to see the tower lit up, and use night mode with your phone braced against a post or your chest.
card.selfie_here: Try the Torch of Friendship at the northwest corner of Bayfront Park, beside the curved wall of country seals on the Biscayne Boulevard side. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold it low so the tower sits over your shoulder, down the boulevard. The tower is about 1,200 feet northwest of the monument, but check it's in view before you pose.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the sidewalk opposite the tower, across from the Kaseya Center, where they can step back far enough to fit the whole building in, while you pose in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks and similar devices are prohibited under the Freedom Tower's visitor guidelines, though the page doesn't say whether that covers the outdoor area. Stay on the pavement and keep clear of traffic.
card.challenge: Wait for a gap in the cars, then snap the tower dead-straight on a gridline with the whole road leading to it.
card.good_to_know: The tower was built in 1925 as the home of The Miami News, and its design borrows from the Giralda in Seville. In the 1960s it was used to process and help refugees arriving from Cuba, which earned it National Historic Landmark status in 2008. It reopened in September 2025 after a long restoration and is now a museum, so check the official site for current access to the inside.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Biscayne Boulevard, on the pavement in front of the Freedom Tower's east façade, and face the tower so the wide road leads the eye to it.

card.hook: You'll see it before you reach it: a tall bronze hand rising out of a still pool, covered in tiny climbing figures. It's a quiet, powerful place, and even a quick phone shot works.
card.stand_here: Stand on Meridian Avenue at the corner with Dade Boulevard, by the memorial's street frontage, and face south-east toward the hand. You'll get the tall hand with the pool and greenery around it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the hand, the pool and the greenery. Go to zoom 0.5x for more of the pool and surroundings, but keep the hand away from the edges of the frame so it doesn't stretch. Try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the figures on the arm.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the hand, then drag the brightness slider down a little so the sky doesn't wash out the dark bronze.
card.best_time: Go when the memorial is open and the light is soft, in the morning or later in the day. Hours can vary, so check the official site before you head over.
card.selfie_here: Try the path beside the dark water at the edge of the pool, with the hand rising behind you. The stone tunnel on the walkway just before the island also frames your approach. Use the front camera, and zoom 0.5x if you want more of the hand in the shot. We couldn't confirm which way to face in either spot, so check on site.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the street side at the corner of Meridian Avenue and Dade Boulevard and frame you with the hand and the memorial behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photos are welcome, but photoshoots need permission. Keep your phone use to a minimum, keep your photos quiet, and avoid other visitors in the frame. Pets, bicycles, scooters and Segways aren't allowed on the grounds.
card.challenge: Find the spot where the arm and its reflection in the pool both fit in one frame, then take the shot quietly and level, so the arm stands straight.
card.good_to_know: This is a solemn, open-air memorial of remembrance. Its most striking feature is a tall bronze arm and hand reaching up out of a pool, covered in climbing figures. It's on Meridian Avenue at Dade Boulevard, near the Convention Center, and it's a free spot.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Meridian Avenue at the corner with Dade Boulevard, by the memorial's street frontage, and face south-east toward the hand. You'll get the tall hand with the pool and greenery around it.

card.hook: Do a slow lap of the Bass Museum before you snap anything. The walls, doorways and shadows reward a few minutes of looking, and your first quick shot is rarely your best.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Bass Museum, right where the phone icon sits on the map. Face the main entrance, then step back a few paces so the whole building fits.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural look at the building. If you're too close to the walls to step back, tap 0.5x. For doorways, signs and textures, try 2x or 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the walls up with them, so the building stands straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon gives softer light and gentler shadows on the walls than the middle of the day.
card.selfie_here: Head to Ugo Rondinone's Miami Mountain, the five stacked painted boulders in Collins Park beside the museum. Use the front camera, tap 0.5x if you can, and stand in front of the boulders so the bright colours fill the background and the Bass is in view nearby.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the park lawn facing the main entrance, while you stand near the entrance, so the whole building fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photos are generally allowed inside, and flash is the most common restriction. Selfie sticks are typically not allowed in the galleries, so check on the day.
card.challenge: Wait for a gap in the crowd and get one clean shot of the entrance with nobody in it, then one close-up of a doorway framed by plants.

card.hook: A big, nearly windowless wall is a funny thing to fall for, but that's the charm of the Wolfsonian–FIU. It gives you strong lines and one clear subject, so framing it is easy.
card.stand_here: Stand on the pavement outside the Wolfsonian–FIU, right where the phone icon sits on the map. It marks the building itself, so there's no hunting for a viewing spot. Face the front and step back as far as the pavement lets you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x and step back until the whole front sits inside the gridlines. If the pavement is too narrow, switch to zoom 0.5x. Then move closer and try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the entrance and surface textures.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the building, then slide the brightness down a little (darker) if the sky is bright, so the front doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Pick a time when the sun lights the front instead of leaving it in shadow. Early morning or late afternoon light is usually softer, so check how it falls when you arrive.
card.selfie_here: Try the sidewalk along Washington Avenue, in front of the museum's nearly windowless facade. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it, and keep the wall over your shoulder. It's a best guess for a backdrop, so check the angle when you get there.
card.rules_and_safety: The street outside is public pavement. Check the official site for visiting details before you go.
card.challenge: Take three shots: one wide of the whole front, one at an angle along the street, and one close-up of a detail. Then see which one your friends like best.
card.good_to_know: The Wolfsonian–FIU is a museum building, and the photo here is about its frontage, entrance and the street around it. It sits at 1001 Washington Avenue, at the corner of 10th Street. Keep your phone level so the vertical edges stay upright.

card.hook: Picture a shaded corner of Calle Ocho where the loudest thing is a domino slamming onto a table, and nobody looks up. That's Máximo Gómez Park, which locals just call "Domino Park".
card.stand_here: Follow the map to the phone icon, which sits right at the subject, in the small green park on Calle Ocho (SW 8th Street). Stay on the public edge outside the fenced game area and face the covered domino tables.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the main wide shot. If you're squeezed for space, drop to 0.5x to fit in the tables, trees and murals. For close details from further back, try zoom 2x or higher, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the covered tables in the middle third, and let the trees and murals fill the sides.
card.best_time: Late morning is when the street activity is strongest. A weekday morning is likely to feel quieter and less touristy.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the tall green trees with the park behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x to fit more of the scene in. Keep to the public side of the fence.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to take your photo from the sidewalk near the corner of SW 8th Street and SW 14th Avenue, and ask them to keep the domino games in the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The tables are reserved for club members, so watch from outside the fenced game area. Ask first before any close portrait, and accept a no with a smile. Summer afternoons can top 90°F (32°C) with little shade, so bring water if you visit then.
card.challenge: Find the painted-domino pavers at the park entrance and shoot them so they lead the eye toward the tables.
card.good_to_know: The park is named after a hero of Cuba's War of Independence. Since the early 1970s, Cuban immigrants have met here to drink coffee, smoke cigars and play dominoes. It also hosts food tours, art festivals and other cultural events.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Follow the map to the phone icon, which sits right at the subject, in the small green park on Calle Ocho (SW 8th Street). Stay on the public edge outside the fenced game area and face the covered domino tables.

selfie_research.notes: Only one selfie spot is supported by a page: the flytographer guide names the covered tables and tall trees, but it does not say the landmark is directly behind the visitor. The bust of Máximo Gómez at the entrance (ParkMagnet photo caption) and the 1994 Summit of the Americas mural (Traverica) were found but no page recommends them as selfie spots, so I left them out. The ask-someone spot is the only corner the pages name, so it is a best available location rather than a confirmed framing point. No page states rules on selfie sticks or tripods. Pages advise asking permission before close-up photos of players (Roami, Traverica, Nomado), which is a people-photography etiquette point, not a selfie-stick rule, so I did not list it under rules. The park is listed at 801 SW 15th Ave (Yelp), and minube places it between SW 8th Street and SW 15th Avenue.
